plan:
1. Offer that protective part the same Nurturer voice you meant for your little one, not a harder one. If you can't find that voice in yourself yet, borrow it from someone safe. Then ask it what it's afraid would happen if it stepped back. Its answer might be a fear that this will turn into one more performance you'll fool yourself with, or that the pain would be too much, or that you've tried before and it can't take another letdown; one answer a reader would recognize is enough.
2. Take the fear in before you answer it. It may be describing your history accurately. Here the Nurturer is there to receive what that part has been carrying, not to win an argument with it.
3. The Protector, the grown-up's own function, earns that part's trust in ordinary life, with things you actually do that make your life safer, like keeping a promise to yourself or setting a boundary (one or two acts; don't tell the reader to leave a situation: Joel finds "leave it" too simple, and the article deals with it elsewhere). Over time, what you do is what convinces it that a trustworthy adult has shown up; one kind talk inside your head usually won't outweigh years of evidence the other way.
4. Usually it's only after that part feels heard that your little one comes forward. Push past the guards and you may get a convincing performance of the work, the right words, maybe even tears, while nothing underneath feels any safer. The protective part doesn't have to go away: it can keep watch while it lets one small step happen, as long as you stay present and can stop. And if it says no, that's a no.
5. Then follow what changes, like a critic softening into a fear, or a vague hurt turning into a clear need. Respond to what's there now instead of starting the exercise over. When a need gets clear, try offering that kind of care and notice how it lands. You don't need an age or a memory to work with a feeling, and a small shift counts; more intensity isn't the only way forward.
established:
- Start With Whatever Showed Up says a reaction that shows up when you go looking for your little one counts as part of the work, and it may be a part of you that's trying to protect you. It already gives the reader a line to say to that part, "I see you. I'm not going to force my way past you. What's going on?", then says to wait and listen, that it's fine if nothing comes, and to only do what a part tells you if it's loving and leaves you free. Don't repeat that line or those steps.
- Two Common Protective Patterns (just before this) describes the kind that's always on duty (a skeptic: "You're just making this up") and the kind that shows up near pain (a sudden pull to do anything but feel it), says both started out trying to prevent something that really hurt, and ends on treating either one like an enemy giving it one more reason to stay in charge: "I wonder what it would do if it didn't have to."
- Core terms the reader knows: "your little one" (the inner child); the grown-up's three functions, the Nurturer, the Protector and the Guide; "borrowed adulthood" (getting a grown-up function from someone else first, like warmth from someone you remember); pl/ork. "The Protector" is the grown-up's own protecting function; a protective response is "a part of you that's trying to protect you" or "a protective part", never "the Protector". Keep the two apart wherever both come up.
limits:
- Not numbered steps, and not one paragraph per step: the guide lays this out as a sequence, and a sequence written out sentence by sentence is exactly what reads as code instructions put into English (Joel, 2026-10-03: "the marching order"). Say it as the narrator would, in four or five paragraphs that each stop somewhere to react, wonder, allow something, or just stay with it.
- No list of three or more in one sentence (Joel, 2026-10-03: "lists of 3 in general are an ai pattern"). If a list doesn't need all its items, keep the one or two that matter most; if every item matters, give each its own sentence.
- Plain words. Invent nothing about Joel's life, and no made-up scene longer than a small example.
- Every sentence has to work for a reader who doesn't remember anything from sections back; core terms are fine.
- If a point seems to need one more condition, make the paragraph simpler rather than longer.
after: The next part of the article, "When to Change the Strategy", starts: if you keep trying something and not much seems to change, don't decide right away that the whole method has failed.
